learn: Energy is the ability to cause change or do work.
Moving objects have kinetic energy. Stored energy is potential energy, like a stretched rubber band or a ball at the top of a hill.
Energy can change from one form to another but is never created or destroyed.
lessons.try: Roll a ball down ramps of different heights and observe how far it goes.

learn: The faster an object moves, the more kinetic energy it has.
A ball rolled from higher up gains more speed and energy.
A faster bowling ball knocks down more pins because it has more energy.
check: A ball from higher up gains...
lessons.try: Drop a ball from 30 cm and 90 cm onto sand. Compare the craters.

learn: When objects collide, energy transfers between them.
Some energy changes into sound and heat during a collision.
Engineers design bumpers and helmets to absorb collision energy.
lessons.try: Roll one marble into another and observe what happens.

learn: Energy is the ability to make things move or change.
Forms include motion, heat, light, sound, electrical and chemical energy.
Energy is everywhere.
check: Energy is the ability to make things...
Which is a form of energy?
lessons.try: List one example of each form of energy at school.

learn: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.
Anything moving has kinetic energy.
Faster objects have more.
check: A parked car has ___ kinetic energy.
lessons.try: Roll balls at different speeds and compare.

learn: Stored (potential) energy waits to be used.
A stretched rubber band, a raised ball and a battery store energy.
Stored energy can turn into motion.
check: A stretched rubber band has ___ energy.
lessons.try: Launch a toy with a rubber band.

learn: The faster an object moves, the more energy it has.
A fast ball knocks over more pins than a slow one.
Speed and energy are linked.
check: A fast ball knocks over ___ pins.
lessons.try: Roll a ball at two speeds into cups and measure how far they move.

learn: Objects lifted higher store more energy.
Dropped from higher, they hit harder.
Roller coasters start with a big hill.
check: Roller coasters start with a big...
lessons.try: Drop a ball from different heights onto clay and measure dents.

learn: Energy moves from one object to another.
A bat transfers energy to a ball.
The bat slows; the ball speeds up.
check: A bat ___ energy to a ball.
Energy moves from one ___ to another.
lessons.try: Use Newton's cradle or marbles to see energy transfer.

learn: A collision is when objects hit each other.
Energy transfers in collisions.
Some energy becomes sound and heat.
lessons.try: Collide toy cars and observe.

learn: Collisions can change speed, direction or shape.
A heavy ball hitting a light ball sends it fast.
Crumple zones in cars absorb energy.
check: A heavy ball hitting a light ball sends it...
lessons.try: Test collisions between balls of different masses.

learn: Energy is not destroyed; it changes form.
A rolling ball slows because energy becomes heat and sound.
Total energy stays the same.
check: A slowing ball turns energy into heat and...
lessons.try: Rub your hands and feel motion become heat.

learn: Energy changes form in chains.
Sun → plants (chemical) → you (motion).
Draw arrows to show changes.
lessons.try: Draw an energy chain for a bike ride.

learn: Engineers design devices that change energy.
A pinwheel changes wind energy into motion.
A solar oven changes light into heat.
check: A solar oven changes light into...
lessons.try: Design a device that converts one energy form to another.

learn: Energy makes things move and change.
Speed and height affect energy.
Energy transfers and changes form but isn't destroyed.
lessons.try: Build a marble run and explain its energy.

units.t: Energy Transfer: Heat, Light, Sound and Electricity

learn: Heat energy moves from warmer objects to cooler ones.
Conductors, like metal, let heat move easily. Insulators, like wood, plastic and wool, slow heat flow.
A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot; a wooden spoon stays cooler.
check: Which is a good heat conductor?
lessons.try: Place metal, plastic and wooden spoons in warm water. Which handle warms fastest?

learn: Electricity is the flow of electric charge.
A circuit is a complete path for electricity: a battery, wires and a device like a bulb.
In an open circuit, the path is broken and the bulb goes out. A switch opens and closes a circuit.
check: What happens in an open circuit?
lessons.try: Draw a simple circuit with a battery, wires, a switch and a bulb.

learn: Electrical conductors include copper and other metals. Insulators include rubber and plastic.
Wires are copper covered in plastic so electricity flows inside but not to your hand.
Never touch outlets, play near power lines or use electrical devices near water.
check: Should you use electrical devices near water?
lessons.try: Make a home safety checklist for electricity.

learn: Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things.
A hot drink cools; ice melts in your hand.
Heat flows until temperatures are equal.
lessons.try: Put a spoon in hot water and feel the handle warm.

learn: Conduction is heat moving by touch.
A metal pan handle gets hot.
Metals are good heat conductors.
lessons.try: Test which spoons warm fastest: metal, plastic, wood.

learn: Convection is heat moving through liquids and gases as they flow.
Radiation is heat travelling as waves, like sunlight.
You feel radiation from a campfire.
check: Heat from the sun reaches us by...
Campfire warmth on your face is...
lessons.try: Watch food colouring move in warm water.

learn: Insulators slow heat transfer.
Wool, foam, plastic and air are insulators.
Coolers and coats use insulators.
lessons.try: Test which material keeps ice longest.

learn: Light is energy that travels fast.
Light comes from the sun, flames and bulbs.
Light can turn into heat when absorbed.
lessons.try: Compare temperatures of black and white paper in sunlight.

learn: Sound is energy from vibrations.
Sound travels through air, water and solids.
Louder sounds carry more energy.
lessons.try: Make a string telephone.

learn: Electricity is energy from moving charges.
It powers lights, motors and phones.
It can change to light, heat, sound and motion.
check: A light bulb changes electricity into...
lessons.try: List devices and what electricity becomes in each.

learn: A circuit is a complete path for electricity.
It needs a power source, wires and a load like a bulb.
A switch opens or closes the circuit.
lessons.try: Build a simple circuit with a battery and bulb.

learn: In a closed circuit, electricity flows and the bulb lights.
In an open circuit, there's a gap and nothing flows.
Switches create gaps.
check: In a closed circuit, the bulb...
lessons.try: Make a switch from a paper clip.

learn: In a series circuit, there's one path. If one bulb fails, all go out.
In a parallel circuit, there are several paths.
Homes use parallel circuits.
check: If one bulb in series fails, the others...
lessons.try: Build both circuits and test them.

learn: Conductors let electricity flow: metals, salt water.
Insulators block it: rubber, plastic, wood.
Wires are metal inside and plastic outside.
check: Wires are coated in plastic to...
lessons.try: Test materials in a circuit.

learn: Never touch outlets with wet hands.
Don't put objects in sockets.
Stay away from fallen power lines.
lessons.try: Make an electrical safety poster.

learn: A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another.
Waves have crests (high points) and troughs (low points).
Amplitude is the height of a wave. Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next.
check: The high point of a wave is the...
The distance from crest to crest is the...
lessons.try: Shake a rope or slinky to make waves. Change your speed and watch.

learn: Water waves move energy across the surface, but the water itself mostly moves up and down.
Sound travels as waves of vibration through air, water and solids.
Larger amplitude sound waves are louder.
check: In a water wave, the water mostly moves...
lessons.try: Float a cork in a tub and make waves. Does the cork travel across or bob in place?

learn: Patterns of waves can carry information.
Morse code sends messages with long and short signals.
Radio, mobile phones and Wi-Fi send information using invisible waves.
lessons.try: Send a Morse code message to a family member with a flashlight.

learn: A wave is a disturbance that carries energy.
Waves move energy, not matter.
A cork bobs up and down as a wave passes.
check: A cork in a wave moves...
lessons.try: Watch a cork in a tub as you make waves.

learn: The crest is the top. The trough is the bottom.
Amplitude is the height from the middle.
Wavelength is the distance between crests.
check: The top of a wave is the...
The bottom of a wave is the...
lessons.try: Draw and label a wave.

learn: Bigger amplitude means more energy.
Tall ocean waves can knock you over.
Louder sounds have bigger amplitude.
lessons.try: Shake a rope gently and hard. Compare.

learn: Frequency is how many waves pass per second.
Short wavelength = high frequency.
High-pitched sounds have high frequency.
lessons.try: Make fast and slow waves on a spring toy.

learn: Wind makes water waves.
Waves carry energy across oceans.
Waves shape beaches by moving sand.
lessons.try: Make waves in a tray and watch sand move.

learn: Sound waves travel by squeezing and stretching air.
They need a medium: air, water or solid.
Sound can't travel in empty space.
check: Can sound travel in empty space?
lessons.try: Ring a bell in a jar and discuss what happens if air is removed.

learn: Light also travels as waves.
Light doesn't need a medium; it crosses space.
Light is the fastest thing in the universe.
lessons.try: Discuss how sunlight reaches Earth.

learn: An echo is a sound wave bouncing back.
Bats and dolphins use echoes to find food.
This is called echolocation.
check: Echoes happen when sound hits a...
lessons.try: Clap near a wall and listen for an echo.

learn: Earthquakes send waves through Earth.
Seismographs record them.
Scientists study waves to learn about Earth's inside.
lessons.try: Make a simple seismograph with paper and a pen.

learn: Patterns can carry messages: Morse code uses dots and dashes.
Flashing lights, drums and flags send codes.
Patterns travel as waves.
lessons.try: Send a Morse code message with a flashlight.

learn: Computers send information as patterns of 1s and 0s.
Phones turn voices into digital signals and back.
Digital signals travel by radio waves or wires.
check: Digital signals travel by radio waves or...
lessons.try: Encode your name in binary using a chart.

learn: Waves carry energy, not matter.
Amplitude, wavelength and frequency describe waves.
Waves carry information in patterns.
check: The top of a wave is the...
lessons.try: Make a waves concept map.

learn: Light travels in straight lines from a source.
When light hits an object, it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted (pass through).
We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes.
check: Reflects off them into our eyes
lessons.try: Use a flashlight and mirrors to bounce light around a corner.

learn: Light enters the eye through the pupil, the black opening.
The lens focuses light onto the retina at the back of the eye.
The retina sends signals to the brain through the optic nerve.
check: Light enters the eye through the...
Signals go to the brain through the...
lessons.try: In a mirror, watch your pupils change size when you turn on a light.

learn: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one material to another, like air to water.
A straw in water looks bent because of refraction.
A prism splits white light into a rainbow of colours.
check: A prism splits white light into...
lessons.try: Put a pencil in a glass of water and look from the side.

learn: Light sources make their own light: sun, fire, bulbs.
The moon reflects sunlight; it's not a source.
Some animals glow: fireflies.
lessons.try: Sort objects into light sources and not.

learn: Light travels in straight lines.
Shadows form when objects block light.
Light can't bend around corners on its own.
check: Light ___ bend around corners on its own.
lessons.try: Shine a torch through holes in cards lined up.

learn: Moving the light changes the shadow.
Closer to the light = bigger shadow.
Shadows outside change during the day as the sun moves.
check: Closer to the light makes a ___ shadow.
lessons.try: Trace your shadow at 9 a.m., noon and 3 p.m.

learn: Light bounces off surfaces. This is reflection.
Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect clearly.
Rough surfaces scatter light.
check: Light bouncing off a surface is...
lessons.try: Use mirrors to bounce light to a target.

learn: Some surfaces absorb light.
Dark colours absorb more light and get warmer.
Light colours reflect more.
lessons.try: Measure temperatures under black and white cloths.

learn: Transparent materials let light through clearly: glass.
Translucent let some through: wax paper.
Opaque block light: wood.
lessons.try: Test materials with a torch.

learn: We see when light reflects off objects into our eyes.
In total darkness, we see nothing.
Eyes need light.
check: We see when light enters our...
Light reflects off objects into our...
lessons.try: Look at an object in a dark box, then with a small hole lit.

learn: Light enters through the pupil.
The lens focuses light on the retina.
The optic nerve sends signals to the brain.
check: The ___ sends signals to the brain.
lessons.try: Label a diagram of the eye.

learn: The iris controls pupil size.
In bright light, pupils shrink. In dim light, they widen.
This protects the eye and helps it see.
lessons.try: Watch a partner's pupils when lights dim (carefully).

learn: Refraction is light bending as it passes between materials.
A straw looks bent in water.
Lenses use refraction.
lessons.try: Look at a pencil in a glass of water.

learn: White light is a mix of all colours.
A prism splits light into a rainbow.
Objects look coloured because they reflect that colour.
check: White light is a mix of...
A ___ splits light into a rainbow.
lessons.try: Make a rainbow with a prism or water glass.

learn: Light travels straight, reflects, refracts and is absorbed.
We see when light enters our eyes.
White light contains all colours.
check: The lens focuses light on the...
lessons.try: Design a periscope from mirrors and a box.

learn: Living things have structures that help them survive, grow and reproduce.
External structures are outside, like a bird's feathers or a plant's thorns.
Internal structures are inside, like an animal's heart or a plant's xylem tubes that carry water.
lessons.try: List three internal and three external structures of a human.

learn: Roots absorb water and anchor the plant. Stems support and transport.
Leaves capture sunlight to make food through photosynthesis.
Flowers attract pollinators and make seeds; thorns protect from animals.
check: What protects some plants from animals?
lessons.try: Dissect a flower with a grown-up and identify its parts.

learn: Animals have structures for eating, moving, protection and senses.
Owls have large eyes for night vision. Snakes have flexible jaws to swallow large prey.
Many animals have skeletons for support: inside (endoskeleton) or outside (exoskeleton, like insects).
check: Why do owls have large eyes?
lessons.try: Compare the structures of a fish and a bird.

learn: A structure is a body part. Its function is its job.
A bird's wings (structure) let it fly (function).
Every structure has a purpose.
lessons.try: List five structures and their functions.

learn: External structures are outside: skin, fur, claws, shells.
They protect, help move and sense.
A turtle's shell protects it.
lessons.try: Compare external structures of three animals.

learn: Internal structures are inside: heart, lungs, stomach, brain, bones.
They keep the body alive.
The heart pumps blood.
lessons.try: Label a body organ diagram.

learn: Roots anchor plants and absorb water and minerals.
Taproots go deep. Fibrous roots spread wide.
Carrots are taproots we eat.
lessons.try: Compare a carrot and grass roots.

learn: Stems support plants and carry water and food.
Xylem carries water up. Phloem carries food down.
Tree trunks are big stems.
lessons.try: Put celery in coloured water and watch it climb.

learn: Leaves make food using sunlight (photosynthesis).
They have tiny pores called stomata for gas exchange.
Leaf shapes fit environments.
lessons.try: Look at a leaf under a microscope or hand lens.

learn: Flowers are reproductive structures.
Stamens make pollen. The pistil receives it.
Pollinated flowers make seeds and fruit.
lessons.try: Dissect a flower and find stamens and pistil.

learn: Plants protect themselves with thorns, spines, bad tastes and poisons.
Cactus spines keep animals away.
Some plants have thick bark.
lessons.try: List plant defences seen on a walk.

learn: Skeletons support and protect bodies.
Muscles pull on bones to move.
Insects have exoskeletons on the outside.
lessons.try: Feel your muscles work as you bend your arm.

learn: Lungs take in oxygen from air.
Fish use gills to get oxygen from water.
Insects breathe through tiny holes.
lessons.try: Compare how three animals breathe.

learn: Teeth break food. The stomach and intestines digest it.
Bird gizzards grind food.
Different animals have different teeth.
lessons.try: Compare teeth of a herbivore and a carnivore.

learn: Plants and animals have internal and external structures.
Each structure has a function.
Structures help growth, survival, behaviour and reproduction.
lessons.try: Invent a creature and explain each structure.

learn: Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch collect information from the environment.
Each sense organ has receptors: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin.
Receptors turn information into signals sent along nerves.
check: How many basic senses do we list?
lessons.try: Do a blindfolded taste test with a grown-up to explore smell and taste.

learn: The brain receives signals, processes them and decides how to respond.
Nerves carry messages between the brain and body.
Some responses are reflexes that happen automatically, like pulling your hand away from something hot.
lessons.try: Test your reaction time by catching a dropped ruler.

learn: Animals use senses in amazing ways.
Bats and dolphins use echolocation: they make sounds and listen to echoes.
Sharks sense electricity from prey. Dogs have a sense of smell many times stronger than ours.
check: Dogs have a very strong sense of...
lessons.try: Research one animal with a special sense.

learn: Senses collect information about the world.
Sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell.
Senses help us stay safe and find food.
check: How many main senses do people have?
lessons.try: List a time each sense kept you safe.

learn: Eyes detect light and colour.
The brain turns signals into pictures.
Two eyes help judge distance.
lessons.try: Try catching a ball with one eye closed.

learn: Ears collect sound waves.
The eardrum vibrates and tiny bones pass on the vibrations.
Nerves carry signals to the brain.
lessons.try: Model an eardrum with plastic wrap and rice.

learn: Skin has receptors for pressure, heat, cold and pain.
Fingertips have many receptors.
Pain warns of danger.
lessons.try: Test two-point touch on fingers and arm.

learn: The tongue tastes sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury.
Smell is much of what we call flavour.
Hold your nose and food tastes bland.
check: The tongue tastes sweet, salty, sour, bitter and...
Holding your nose makes food taste...
lessons.try: Taste-test with and without holding your nose.

learn: The brain is the body's control centre.
It processes senses, controls movement and stores memories.
It's protected by the skull.
check: The brain is protected by the...
lessons.try: Label main parts of a brain diagram.

learn: Nerves are messengers that carry signals.
The spinal cord connects the brain to the body.
Signals travel very fast.
check: The spinal cord connects the brain to the...
lessons.try: Play a "pass the squeeze" signal game.

learn: Reflexes are automatic actions.
Pulling your hand from a hot stove is a reflex.
Reflexes skip the brain for speed.
check: Pulling away from heat is a...

lessons.try: Test the knee-jerk reflex gently.

learn: The brain stores information as memories.
Practice turns short-term memories into long-term ones.
Sleep helps memory.
lessons.try: Try memorising a list with and without practice.

learn: Some animals sense things humans can't.
Bats hear echoes. Snakes sense heat. Sharks sense electricity.
Senses fit animals' needs.
lessons.try: Make a chart of super senses.

learn: Animals use senses to find food, avoid danger and find mates.
A rabbit hears a hawk and freezes.
Information leads to action.
check: A rabbit hearing a hawk will...
lessons.try: Describe the sense → brain → action path for an animal.

learn: Senses gather information; nerves carry it; the brain decides.
Reflexes are fast and automatic.
Animals have amazing senses.
lessons.try: Build a senses stations circuit.

learn: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces.
Physical weathering includes ice wedging: water freezes in cracks, expands and splits rock.
Chemical weathering happens when water and air change the minerals in rock, like rust.
lessons.try: Shake rough rocks in a jar of water and watch them become smoother over days.

learn: Erosion moves weathered rock and soil to new places.
Water, wind, ice (glaciers) and gravity cause erosion.
Deposition is when the material is dropped in a new place, like a river delta.
check: Dropping material in a new place is...
lessons.try: Build a sand hill and pour water on it. Where does the sand go?

learn: The Grand Canyon was carved by the Colorado River over millions of years.
Glaciers carved U-shaped valleys. Wind shapes sand dunes and arches.
Plant roots can slow erosion by holding soil.
lessons.try: Compare pictures of a V-shaped river valley and a U-shaped glacier valley.

learn: Weathering is the breaking of rock into smaller pieces.
It happens slowly over time.
Weathering doesn't move rock; erosion does.
lessons.try: Shake chalk pieces in a jar of water.

learn: Physical weathering breaks rock without changing what it is made of.
Ice wedging: water freezes in cracks and splits rock.
Roots and wind-blown sand also break rock.
check: Water freezing in cracks is ice...
Physical weathering ___ change what rock is made of.
lessons.try: Freeze a water-filled straw in clay.

learn: Chemical weathering changes rock into new materials.
Acid rain dissolves limestone.
Rust weakens iron-rich rocks.
check: Chemical weathering ___ rock into new materials.
lessons.try: Drop vinegar on chalk and watch it fizz.

learn: Rivers carry sediment downstream.
Rain washes soil off slopes.
Fast water erodes more.
lessons.try: Pour water down sand slopes at different speeds.

learn: Wind picks up and carries sand and dust.
It shapes sand dunes and rock arches.
Dry places have more wind erosion.
check: Wind erosion is strongest where it's...
lessons.try: Blow across sand with a fan.

learn: Glaciers are slow rivers of ice.
They scrape and carry rocks.
They carve U-shaped valleys.
lessons.try: Push ice with sand under it across clay.

learn: Deposition is dropping sediment in a new place.
Rivers deposit sediment at deltas.
Wind deposits sand to make dunes.
lessons.try: Model a river delta in a tray.

learn: Gravity pulls rock and soil downhill.
Landslides and mudslides are fast.
Creep is slow movement over years.
lessons.try: Model a landslide with wet and dry soil.

learn: The Grand Canyon was carved by the Colorado River over millions of years.

Water and time make canyons.
check: The Grand Canyon was carved by the ___ River.

learn: Waves erode cliffs and deposit sand.
Beaches change shape with storms and seasons.

Plants and engineering reduce erosion.

Scientists read rock layers like pages in a history book.
check: In rock layers, the oldest are usually at the...
lessons.try: Make layers of different coloured sand in a jar.

Index fossils help scientists match layers in different places.
check: Marine fossils in a desert show...
lessons.try: Look at a diagram of rock layers with fossils and describe the area's history.

Scientists use evidence to explain how landscapes changed.
check: Rock layers can be bent by...
lessons.try: Fold layers of clay to model how rock layers bend.

learn: Igneous rock forms from cooled lava or magma.
Sedimentary rock forms from layers of sediment.
Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change rock.

check: The oldest layer is at the...
The youngest layer is at the...

check: Layers are like pages of Earth's...
lessons.try: Interpret a rock layer diagram.

check: Different fossils in layers show life...

lessons.try: Sort fossil cards into layers by age.

learn: Mountains rise, wear down and rise again.

Landscapes change over millions of years.

learn: Layers form in order with the oldest at the bottom.

Folds and faults change layers.

check: Magma that reaches the surface is...
lessons.try: Draw and label a cross-section of a volcano.

check: Volcanoes and earthquakes often line up in...
lessons.try: Mark volcanoes and earthquakes on a world map.

check: The crust is thin like an apple's...

check: Plates move about a few ___ a year.
lessons.try: Make a plate puzzle map.
